html:
After the Haitian Revolution ruined the sugar of Saint-Domingue in the 1790s, Cuba took its place, and by the mid 1800s it was the largest sugar producer in the world.

Planters imported hundreds of thousands of Africans in the Atlantic slave trade, long after Britain had banned it. They also brought in Chinese contract labourers, and built steam mills and Latin America's first railway in 1837.

Sugar shaped Cuba's society and politics for two centuries: its slavery, its wars, and its dependence on the United States and then the Soviet Union, which bought the crop at high prices after the revolution. When Soviet aid ended in the Special Period, the industry collapsed, and many mills closed in 2002.
sum: After the Haitian Revolution ruined the sugar of Saint-Domingue in the 1790s, Cuba took its place, and by the mid 1800s it was the largest sugar producer in the world.
